title: How Public Broadcasting Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain how public broadcasting in the United States works, covering its origins in early radio and the commercial model, the Public Broadcasting Act of 1967 and the creation of the Corporation for Public Broadcasting (CPB), how funding flows from taxpayers through CPB to local member stations and then to NPR and PBS, the debate over bias and government funding (including the Cato Institute critique, the Duke study, and Trump's proposed defunding), the shift to podcasts and on-demand media, Sesame Street's move to HBO, and a listener mail item about refrigerating ketchup.

segments.title: Opening banter and introduction
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with banter about beans and musical fruit, praise Terry Gross and Jesse Thorn's The Turnaround, and introduce public broadcasting as the topic, noting its large audience of more than half of Americans.

segments.title: Origins of public broadcasting and the commercial model
segments.summary: Radio's rise as a mass medium led Europe and the UK to treat it as a public good funded publicly, while the US Radio Act and Communications Act set up a competitive commercial system. Broadcasting drifted toward entertainment for advertising money, and by the fifties people sought an alternative.

segments.title: Local news nostalgia and the news landscape
segments.summary: The hosts discuss declining interest in network and local TV news, cable news, and getting news from social media, reminiscing about Los Angeles and Atlanta local news personalities.

segments.title: Lyndon Johnson, NET and the Public Broadcasting Act
segments.summary: Johnson signed the Public Broadcasting Act of 1967. Its precursor, National Educational Television (NET), ran programming critical of government and foreign policy, and some say this helped motivate government funding. The Corporation for Public Broadcasting was created, which funds rather than produces programming.

segments.title: How public funding flows to NPR and PBS
segments.summary: CPB's budget of about 445 million dollars, roughly a tiny fraction of the federal budget, is distributed mainly to small local stations, which pay licensing fees to carry NPR and PBS programs. NPR began with about ninety member stations and now has close to a thousand. Revenue also comes from station fees, corporate sponsorship, grants, foundations such as Ford, Carnegie-style endowments, and listeners, with station fees scaled to listenership and revenue.

segments.title: PBS reach and history of shows
segments.summary: PBS has around 350 member stations in all fifty states plus Guam, Puerto Rico, the US Virgin Islands, and American Samoa, receiving about seven percent of its funding from CPB. Shows mentioned include Mister Rogers' Neighborhood, NOVA, Masterpiece Theatre, This Old House, Sesame Street, and Antiques Roadshow.

segments.title: Perceived bias and the Cato critique
segments.summary: Critics such as David Boaz of the Cato Institute argue public broadcasting transfers wealth from taxpayers to produce programming mostly consumed by the upper middle class. The 2011 Vivian Schiller resignation after an undercover video is discussed, along with a Duke University study placing NPR left of center but right of several outlets. NPR cited survey data showing its audience is mixed.

segments.title: Chomsky critique and Trump's proposed defunding
segments.summary: Noam Chomsky's critique that public media stays within the status quo is presented. The hosts then discuss Trump's budget proposal calling for eventual elimination of federal funding for PBS, NPR and CPB, and the risk to rural small-market stations. They compare New Zealand's TVNZ deregulation and the BBC's funding model.

segments.title: Podcasts, audience age, and local affiliate survival
segments.summary: NPR's median audience age has risen, and NPR podcasts such as Hidden Brain, This American Life, Planet Money, Serial and Ted Radio Hour rank highly on iTunes. Concerns are raised that podcasts may pull listeners away from local affiliates that depend on donations. The hosts suggest alternative models and discuss the NPR app and Passport.

segments.title: Sesame Street moves to HBO and closing facts
segments.summary: Sesame Street moved to HBO after forty-six years on PBS, with new episodes airing on PBS nine months later. The hosts share facts about NPR's first broadcast covering Vietnam War protests, Susan Stamberg, Tiny Desk Concerts, and a 2011 study on Western democracies.

segments.title: Listener mail: ketchup refrigeration
segments.summary: Listener Aaron writes that Heinz's fridge-fit ketchup bottle marketing led to the idea that ketchup belongs in the refrigerator. The hosts read the email and sign off with contact information.
